title: Valladolid Festival Prizes: Alain Gomis’ ‘Dao’ Wins Golden Spike, ‘La Gradiva’ Takes Silver
full_text: × Nov 1, 2026 5:02am PT Valladolid Festival Prizes: Alain Gomis’ ‘Dao’ Wins Golden Spike, ‘La Gradiva’ Takes Silver Lisandro Alonso earns best director honors, and Alba Rohrwacher and Swann Arlaud receive acting prizes, while Claudia Estrada Tarascó’s 'Salen las lobas' emerged as one of the festival's discoveries By Emiliano de Pablos Plus Icon Emiliano de Pablos Latest South Boost: María Ripoll and Max Lemcke Feature in a Project Lineup Reflecting Andalusia’s Growing TV Ambitions 5 days ago Valladolid Film Festival Draws Global Auteurs, 30 World Premieres and Emerging Spanish Talent 1 week ago Fueled by ‘La Bola Negra,’ Spain’s Indie Distribution Make Robust Gains, to Be Highlighted at Valladolid’s Merci Market 1 week ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Dao' Courtesy of Valladolid International Film Festival French-Senegalese filmmaker Alain Gomis ’ “ Dao ,” an expansive family saga spanning Europe and Africa, was awarded the Golden Spike for best film at Spain’s 71st Valladolid International Film Festival ( Seminci ) while Marine Atlan’s acclaimed debut “ La Gradiva ” received the Silver Spike. Unfolding between a wedding in France and an ancestral memorial ceremony in Guinea-Bissau, Gomis’ three-hour film blurs fiction and documentary, gathering a sprawling cast of professional and non-professional performers to explore family ties, migration and the pull of inherited traditions. The international jury praised the film’s distinctive cinematic form, citing its use of rhythm, duration and movement to create an intimate yet immersive atmosphere. Related Stories Producer Will Packer Stumps to Get Out the Vote and Launch a Private HBCU Fundraising Campaign Bill Maher Fact-Checks Kid Rock After He Compares Abdul El-Sayed to 9/11 Hijackers on ‘Real Time’ “Dao,” which world premiered in competition at Berlin, marks Gomis’ return to fiction features after “Félicité,” winner of the 2017 Berlinale Grand Jury Prize. Reviewing the new film, Variety ’s Guy Lodge called it the director’s “most vibrantly expansive and accessible” work. The Party Film Sales handles international sales while Janus Films holds North American distribution rights. Atlan’s “La Gradiva” premiered at Cannes’ Critics’ Week, where it won its top Grand Prix, before receiving the Melbourne International Film Festival’s Bright Horizons Award in August. At Valladolid, the French-Italian feature also picked up the José Salcedo editing prize for Guillaume Lillo and the Rainbow Spike, recognizing LGBTQ-related cinema. ‘La Gradiva’ Courtesy of Valladolid International Film Festival Set during a French school trip to Naples and Pompeii, the film follows a group of teenagers navigating desire, insecurity and the last moments of adolescence. “Seismically sensitive and deeply moving,” wrote Variety critic Jessica Kiang, who called it “one of the most piercingly accurate and immersive portrayals ever” of that precarious age. MK2 Films represents international sales. Argentine filmmaker Lisandro Alonso, whose credits include “Jauja” and “Eureka,” earned the Ribera del Duero best director award for “Double Freedom,” the well-received sequel to his 2001 debut “Freedom,” sold by Luxbox. Acting honors went to Alba Rohrwacher for Stéphane Brizé’s “A Good Little Soldier,” in which she plays a corporate executive caught in a system of profit at any cost, and Swann Arlaud for Emmanuel Marre’s “A Man of His Time,” about a French engineer drawn into the Vichy regime. Marre’s film also picked up the cinematography award for Olivier Boonjing. Austrian filmmaker Sandra Wollner won the Miguel Delibes screenplay prize for “Everytime,” a drama exploring grief and memory through digital technology. The official competition jury gave a special mention to Tiago Guedes’ “Aquí.” Beyond the main competition, Thai filmmaker Sompot Chidgasornpongse took the Meeting Point prize for “9 Temples to Heaven,” which premiered in Cannes’ Directors’ Fortnight. The contemplative family pilgrimage drama marks the fiction-feature debut of a longtime collaborator of Apichatpong Weerasethakul. Marc Ferrer’s “Cinemanía” received the Fundos Award, while Manon Coubia won the ESCAC directing prize for “Forest High.” Spanish debut “Salen las lobas” emerged as a double audience favorite, taking both the Meeting Point Audience Award and the Seminci Youth Prize. Directed by Claudia Estrada Tarascó, the film follows girls in a juvenile justice facility who bond over music and dreams of a Barcelona trap competition. Produced by Alba Sotorra’s Oceanika, it is sold internationally by MoreThan Films and is set for a Dec. 11 Spanish theatrical release through Silencio Cinema. In the Alchemies section, Ivan Marković’s “Promised Spaces,” a portrait of Cambodia’s rapidly transformed urban landscape, collected the Grand Prize. David Baute’s “Benigno,” about an elderly man preserving a disappearing way of life in the Canary Islands, received a special mention and the environmental Green Spike. Hassen Ferhani’s Algeria-France production “Alea Jacarandas” took the Time of History Grand Prize, with the special award going to Mariano Llinás’ “Life of Jorge Luis Borges.” Isabelle Stever’s “I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming” received the FIPRESCI critics’ prize, while Markus Schleinzer’s “Rose” won the main competition Audience Award. Seminci unveiled its winners Saturday morning in Valladolid after organizers canceled the traditional closing gala following a deadly train accident in Toledo province. Held Oct. 23-31, the festival’s 71st edition was led by interim co-directors Mariona Viader and Javier H. Estrada following the death of José Luis Cienfuegos last December. Organizers reported a provisional audience tally of 100,000, more than 120 film discussions and participation by over 90% of the directors represented in its official sections. title: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Crashes Into Tokyo Film Festival With Stars Ryunosuke Kamiki, Minami Hamabe in Tow
full_text: × Skip to main content By Patrick Brzeski Plus Icon Patrick Brzeski Asia Bureau Chief View All November 1, 2026 1:57am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Godzilla Minus Zero, Godzilla, 2026. GKIDS/Courtesy Everett Collection The King of Monsters finally stomped his way into Japan ’s largest celebration of cinema on Sunday as Takashi Yamazaki ’s wildly anticipated Godzilla Minus Zero played to a packed pair of screenings at the Tokyo International Film Festival. The sold-out shows easily drew the liveliest crowds of this year’s Tokyo festival — the latest Toho -backed monster epic doesn’t open commercially in Japan until Nov. 3 — with numerous die-hard kaiju fans attending in costume or carrying their own Gojira figurines into the theater. Related Stories Music Macklemore Wraps Up Free Palestine Tour in London: "It Was More Uncomfortable for Me to Stay Silent" Movies 'Fuxi: Four Tales of Feasting' Review: Whimsical Chinese Film Explores Myth and History Through a Series of Tasty Treats Godzilla Minus Zero is playing as the “centerpiece film” of the Tokyo festival’s programming this year, and it undoubtedly brought a welcome jolt of energy to the event as it moves through its second half. When the credits rolled on the second screening inside Hulic Hall Tokyo, the crowd erupted into uncharacteristically rapturous applause, with the always respectful but typically subdued Japanese festivalgoers all smiles and excited chatter over favorite monster moments as they poured into the autumn evening in Tokyo’s Ginza district — where much of the carnage on screen takes place. Godzilla Minus Zero is a direct follow-up to Godzilla Minus One (2023), which Yamazaki famously wrote, directed and VFX-supervised. The film was a smash with both critics and mainstream moviegoers, making history as the highest-grossing live-action Japanese film ever in North America ($57.1 million) and later becoming the first film in the multi-decade Godzilla franchise to take home an Oscar, winning the best visual effects award despite competing in the category against Hollywood tentpoles with vastly bigger budgets. The sequel picks up in 1949, two years after the events of Minus One , as Japan struggles to rebuild from the devastation of war and Godzilla’s attack. The Shikishima family’s hard-won peace is threatened by a new calamity, with the film also bringing iconic franchise rival King Ghidorah, the three-headed kaiju, into Yamazaki’s postwar world. Yamazaki’s return to the helm for the follow-up has lifted expectations across the globe — and the critical response so far, along with the enthusiastic reception at home in Tokyo on Sunday, suggests he delivered. Godzilla Minus Zero premiered in September at the New York Film Festival, where The Hollywood Reporter ’s chief critic David Rooney gave it a rave , calling the film a “radioactive blast” and “a crackling kaiju epic every bit as exciting as its predecessor.” The movie currently holds a score of 92 percent on Rotten Tomatoes from 52 reviews. Godzilla Minus Zero ’s two leads, Ryunosuke Kamiki and Minami Hamabe, took the stage to introduce the Tokyo festival screenings and share a few words with fans. Kamiki told the audience he was both “excited” and “a little bit scared” because he could “feel people’s anticipation building as the film’s opening is now very close.” Hamabe added that the first film was so “beloved by fans all over the world, that now for the sequel, well, we need it to be even bigger and better.” “I’m just curious to see how people will receive it,” she added. ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ stars Ryunosuke Kamiki, Sae Nagatani and Minami Hamabe. The duo then welcomed to the stage child actress Sae Nagatani, who plays their characters’ adopted daughter, Akiko. “Together, we play the Shikishima family, and that wouldn’t be complete without our Akiko,” Kamiki said as the little girl joined them and said hello to the audience. “Having a family usually makes us stronger, but it can also make us vulnerable,” Kamiki then said, launching into a bit of plot preview. “[Our family] is trying to always think of family first. But when Godzilla appears, we have to try to protect the family and that leads to some very hard decisions.” Added Hamabe: “I’m very happy to to have met you all here today, and I hope you will enjoy the story of what happens to the Shikishima family — and also, the Godzilla experience, of course!” GKIDS opens Godzilla Minus Zero in cinemas across North America on Nov. 6, following Imax early-access screenings on Nov. 3. title: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Stars Relive Hollywood Ovation and Fan Chants for Yamazaki Takashi at Tokyo Festival
full_text: × Oct 31, 2026 10:18pm PT ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Stars Relive Hollywood Ovation and Fan Chants for Yamazaki Takashi at Tokyo Festival By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Stars Relive Hollywood Ovation and Fan Chants for Yamazaki Takashi at Tokyo Festival 10 hours ago Tokyo Asian Future Drama ‘Jani Be Good’ Probes Silence and Motherhood in a Chinese-Indonesian Family, Marking Ariani Darmawan’s Return 16 hours ago ‘Before the Rain’ Director Milcho Manchevski on Tokyo Competition Title ‘Sister Brother Manhole Cover,’ Whistleblowing and the ‘Death of Beauty’ in Cinema 16 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Naman Ramachandran The cast of “ Godzilla Minus Zero ” brought the glow of a Hollywood standing ovation to the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival on Sunday, two days before Yamazaki Takashi’s follow-up to his Oscar-winning “Godzilla Minus One” opens in Japan. Kamiki Ryunosuke, who returns as lead character Shikishima Koichi, and Hamabe Minami, who reprises the role of his wife Noriko, had flown back to Japan only two days earlier from the film’s premiere at Los Angeles’ TCL Chinese Theatre. Related Stories 'The Mosquito Bowl': How a Parrot Proved to Be Peter Berg's Biggest Challenge ‘It: Welcome to Derry’ Surprise Halloween Episode Drops on HBO Max “The energy was simply extraordinary,” Kamiki said. “Feeling that raw enthusiasm firsthand made me realize all over again just how deeply Godzilla is loved around the world. It was an invaluable experience.” Applause in the 900-seat theater reportedly ran on without a break. Hamabe said the cast later met premiere-goers at an after-party, where many approached them with big smiles to share their reactions. Some had dressed in Godzilla-themed outfits or wore Godzilla badges. The red carpet was open to passersby, Kamiki recalled. Some fans held up large posters and asked for autographs, while chants of the director’s first name broke out from the crowd. “It wasn’t just a polite ‘Takashi,’” he said. “It was like: ‘TAKASHI! HEY, TAKASHI!’ It was roaring.” When Yamazaki went over to sign autographs, the crowd erupted again, leaving Kamiki convinced that “Takashi of the world is truly amazing.” The Tokyo event also marked the first stage appearance of child actor Nagatani Sae, who returns as Shikishima Akiko. Kamiki walked her onstage. In “Minus One,” which aired on Japanese TV’s “Friday Roadshow” on Friday, Akiko’s part consisted mostly of crying or single words such as “Where?” This time, the script gave her full dialogue. “We were like, ‘Really? Can she do this?’” Kamiki said. “But when we got on set, she had all her lines memorized perfectly and delivered them flawlessly.” Hamabe said Nagatani had barely left toddlerhood during the first shoot and was easily frightened by the many adults on set. “So reuniting on this film, I was amazed by how much of a wonderful young girl she had grown into,” she said. “She chatted with us so much, taught me various things, and was very dependable in her acting.” Nagatani said she wasn’t nervous during filming. She recalled Kamiki continuing to rub her back even after the cut was called on a scene in which Akiko cries. She then asked her co-stars how she could become a fine actor while still in elementary school. Kamiki told her she already outshone them both, and said that appearing in both “Minus One” and “Minus Zero” at her age was “an amazing achievement in itself.” According to Kamiki, the new film picks up two years after the events of “Minus One.” “I hope viewers can imagine what those two years were like for them, and see how the family stands together against what comes next,” he said. Hamabe put the gap at two to three years. She said the family had settled into everyday life together before Godzilla resurfaces to threaten it. Asked why the franchise has endured, Kamiki echoed the view of the director and fellow cast members that each Godzilla film mirrors the era in which it is made. “But personally, when I reflect on it, take Godzilla’s existence or the theme music: I cannot even remember when I first heard it or realized, ‘Oh, this is Godzilla’s theme song,’” he said. “It has always been alongside us, which is why I personally think it has remained loved for so long.” Hamabe said that from a human standpoint, Godzilla is overwhelming and impossible to defeat. “Yet, when Godzilla appears, humans unite and stand together to face it,” she said. “I think seeing that human resolve is the first thing that moves people’s hearts.” “Minus One,” the 30th Japanese live-action entry in the Godzilla franchise, grossed more than JPY7.65 billion ($50 million) at the local box office. It became the first Asian production to take home the visual effects prize at the 96th Oscars, and went on to collect more than 50 honors at home and abroad. “Minus Zero” is the first Japanese film to be certified as Filmed for Imax. title: Steep Height? No Sweat: ‘Everest: The Other Side’s Jim Morrison And Jimmy Chin Rappel Down Side Of West Hollywood Building [Video]
full_text: Skip to main content By Matthew Carey Matthew Carey Documentary Editor, Awards @mattcarey More Stories By Matthew Oscar Contender ‘To Hold A Mountain’ To Open In Theaters In December Ahead Of HBO Debut ‘When A Witness Recants’ To Premiere On HBO Soon, Dawn Porter’s Documentary On Shocking Wrongful Conviction Case Inaugural West Hollywood Human Rights Film Festival To Showcase Oscar-Contending Documentaries, 20th Anniversary Screening Of ‘Blood Diamond’ View All October 31, 2026 5:26pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jim Morrison (left, carrying skis) and Jimmy Chin rappel down a billboard in West Hollywood on Friday, October 30, 2026. Matthew Carey Ski mountaineers Jimmy Chin and Jim Morrison are going to great lengths – and heights – to spread the word about the National Geographic documentary Everest: The Other Side . The pair ascended to the top of a 12-story building on the Sunset strip in West Hollywood, CA Friday evening and successfully rappelled down the side. The vertical journey took them along the face of a massive advertisement for the feature film, which opened at 551 theatrical locations on Friday, including IMAX screens. The film, directed by Chin and Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi , shows how Morrison overcame multiple tragedies to achieve the unthinkable – scaling the north side of Mount Everest and then skiing down it, a feat never before accomplished. Related Stories News Everest Doc And 'Breeder' Anchor Indie Frame With Few New Releases - Specialty Preview News Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi & Jimmy Chin Talk 'Everest: The Other Side': "This Is The Most Difficult Film We've Made" - Contenders London “I actually can’t believe how big it is,” Morrison said of the billboard. “It’s huge.” Watch the video of their descent below. Morrison had his skis strapped to his back as he rappelled, but skiing down a right angle, naturally, wasn’t in the plan. “It’s definitely too steep,” he told Deadline. “But it does bring back memories [of Everest] looking down at that part of the line and being on a steep place there with Jimmy this time. It was nice to have him right next to me instead of [filming from] so far away.” Jim Morrison on Mount Everest National Geogrphic Oscar winners Vasarahelyi and Chin’s original intent was to document the quest of Morrison and his life partner, elite ski mountaineer Hilaree Nelson, to summit the dangerous north face of Everest and ski down the formidable Hornbein Couloir. But in September 2022, while on a climbing excursion with Morrison to Manaslu in Nepal, Nelson was killed in an avalanche while skiing down the mountainside. “We were in communication with Jim the whole time” as he grieved, Chin explained during a screening of Everest: The Other Side at the Academy Museum Friday night. “I was with him a lot and we were documenting throughout.” Morrison went through a period of depression after Nelson’s death but rallied and ultimately decided to try to accomplish what he and Nelson had set out to do. For Vasarhelyi, the filmmaking mission became, “How do you honor a story that just got a lot more painful? And also, how do you support Jim through this journey?” Jim Morrison climbs the world’s tallest mountain in ‘Everest: The Other Side’ National Geographic/Jimmy Chin Everest: The Other Side premiered at the Venice Film Festival and then screened at Telluride and Toronto. At Friday night’s Q&A, Morrison shared his reaction to seeing the completed documentary. “The first time I watched it, [producer] Shannon [Dill] and Jimmy came to my hometown and screened it for me and some really close friends of mine. And there was just a tremendous amount of anxiety and I guess stress in the room and tension,” Morrison recalled. “And when it ended, I went up to Jimmy and I put my arms around him and he was crying and I was crying… And he had a real sense of, ‘What [does he] think, what’s about to happen? Does he like it?’ And I just put my arms around him and I said, ‘I lived it, Jimmy. I lived all of it.’” Morrison’s unprecedented ski down the north side of Everest took four hours to complete. At any moment, a wrong move could have been fatal. He spoke to the concentration necessary to accomplish the task. “I’m very focused on putting myself into that space to be sure that I can do it when and if I need to do it,” he said. “I feel very alive when I’m doing that. I feel very connected to the intention of life that I’m living and that I’m living a good life. And for me, it fulfills me. It’s my passion. It’s my drive. It has been since my mom at a very young age pushed me outside and just said, ‘Go outside.’ And I fell in love with nature. And I think there are people that are extraordinarily passionate about their art or their music or going to space — and going to space probably isn’t a really safe endeavor. There’s a whole lot of people that are risking a lot to help that person get to space. But I personally think it’s a good thing for humanity to push the envelope and to strive to do great things and to build great teams to make them happen. And I think it’s valuable and important and I’m really happy that we were able to honor Hilaree in this way by telling the story and achieving the goal and keeping her story alive.” The rappel down the Sunset building, comparatively — that was no sweat. “Rappelling down was a ‘pinch me’ moment,” he said, “but not one I was really afraid of.” Watch the video of Morrison and Chin’s descent below, as well as an interview we did with them immediately afterwards. title: ‘Green Room’ Director Recalls How Patrick Stewart “Saved” Movie From Being Scrapped

Scott Green/A24/Courtesy Everett Collection Logo text Green Room director Jeremy Saulnier paid tribute to Patrick Stewart ahead of a Los Angeles screening of the film on Friday, recalling how the sci-fi icon “just swooped down, nosedived into our cruddy ass movie and saved us.” Celebrating the film’s 10th anniversary, Saulnier addressed the crowd and noted Stewart’s death at 86. “Who’s sad as fuck we lost Patrick Stewart yesterday? Me,” he said in a video posted on the Film Updates X account. “I came here to shamelessly promote Slayground , but instead, I’m just gonna celebrate Patrick Stewart. He had no business doing this movie. He every option to do otherwise.” Related Stories Movies Before 'Star Trek,' Patrick Stewart Proved His Sci-Fi Chops in 'Dune' Critic's Appreciation Patrick Stewart's Career Was a Rare and Thrilling Marriage of the Prestigious and the Populist The director remembered how production on Green Room was “at the point of no return, building sets, and under the gun without Darcy,” noting that the lead character of Darcy Banker had not yet been cast. I left the stage [thinking,] ‘Maybe we’re gonna have to break down the sets and shut the whole movie down.’ Instead, this dude came out of nowhere, from way above our sort of zone, and just swooped down, nosedived into our cruddy ass movie and saved us, and said yes. title: Trump Lawsuit Against Wall Street Journal Over Epstein Story Dismissed by Judge
full_text: × Skip to main content By The Associated Press Plus Icon The Associated Press View All October 31, 2026 5:01pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Donald Trump Courtesy of Getty Saying the president was “grasping at straws,” a federal judge on Saturday threw out Donald Trump ’s $10 billion lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch over a story reporting on his ties to Jeffrey Epstein . U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles in Miami dismissed the suit with prejudice, ruling that the president did not prove the defendants made defamatory statements with actual malice as required by law. The ruling said the lawsuit had attempted to “manufacture” flaws in the Journal ’s investigative reporting. Related Stories TV Bill Maher Responds to Trump's 1,318-Word Social Rant: "He Went Off on Me Like Kelly Clarkson in a Toy Store" Music Canadian Rock Icon Bryan Adams Takes Aim at Trump, Says His Protest Song Gets Standing Ovations in Red States (Exclusive) When a case is thrown out “with prejudice,” it cannot be refiled again and the dismissal is permanent and incontrovertible. The dismissal is a blow to Trump and his administration, which have both pursued adversarial relationships with news organizations during his second term. In addition to the Journal, he is embroiled in lawsuits involving the BBC, The Associated Press and — most recently — CNN, MS NOW and Politico, which are suing him for restored access after he banished them from the White House in mid-September. Trump has denounced media outlets that write things to which he objects and frequently calls them “fake news” and insults their journalists. Trump called the reporting ‘malicious’ The lawsuit against the Journal was over a story it published last year describing a sexually suggestive letter and drawing that the paper said bore Trump’s name and was included in a 2003 album compiled for Epstein’s 50th birthday. The letter was reportedly collected by disgraced British socialite Ghislaine Maxwell as part of a birthday album for Epstein years before he was first arrested in 2006 and subsequently had a falling-out with Trump. The letter bearing Trump’s name includes text framed by the outline of what appears to be a hand-drawn naked woman and ends with, “Happy Birthday — and may every day be another wonderful secret,” according to the newspaper. Trump denied writing it and called the story “false, malicious, and defamatory.” The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Miami, accused the paper and its reporters of having “knowingly and recklessly” published “numerous false, defamatory, and disparaging statements,” which, it alleged, caused “overwhelming financial and reputational harm” to the president. Epstein died by suicide in a New York jail cell in August 2019 while awaiting trial on federal sex trafficking charges. The lawsuit was dismissed once, then refiled Gayles previously dismissed the suit in April, saying Trump had failed to make the argument that the article was published with the intent to be malicious. But he gave the president a chance to file an amended complaint, which he did in May. In Saturday’s ruling, the judge cited the Supreme Court’s landmark 1964 ruling in New York Times Co. v. Sullivan. That decision made it harder for public figures to win libel lawsuits because it requires proof that a media outlet knowingly published something false or showed a reckless disregard for the truth. “The Amended Complaint falls short of pleading actual malice,” Gayles wrote. “Indeed, the allegations regarding malice are conclusory, vague, sometimes inconsistent with the Article, and often irrelevant to whether Defendants knew or should have known that the statements in the Article were purportedly false.” The judge also noted that the Journal’s story did not ignore or minimize Trump’s denial, “Rather, it informed readers that President Trump decried the Letter as a fake and denied writing it.” Gayles also said several other allegations in the lawsuit did not have merit.
